title: Public, internal, confidential: how our data classification works
performance: given an everyday document, file or message, the viewer can name its class (public, internal or confidential), say how that class may be shared, and default to the higher class and ask the owner when unsure

audience.assumed_prior: knows some information is sensitive; has not used the three class names or their handling rules
audience.why: general employee population across roles; the brief's audience.knows
audience.motivation: wants to share quickly without causing a leak; mildly wary of compliance training
audience.context: desktop at work, with sound or captions, a short break between tasks

strategy.name: worked_example_led
strategy.rationale: the classes only mean something applied to real items; one running file (a customer list about to be emailed to a new contractor) carries the lesson and each class is seen on an everyday object before it is named
strategy.signature_move: show an everyday item, ask who could be harmed if it got out, THEN name the class and its handling rule

misconceptions.belief: if it looks harmless it is fine to share outside
misconceptions.why_tempting: most internal items, like meeting notes, contain nothing alarming

misconceptions.belief: the class depends on where the file sits or what format it is in
misconceptions.why_tempting: people associate sensitivity with locked folders or paper stamps

hook.sketch: Your cursor is on Send: a customer list attached, going to a contractor who started this week. Something makes you pause.

arc.promise: three classes and one question sort anything you handle, and the class tells you how to share it
arc.bridge_from_prior: you already sense some things are sensitive; the question 'who could be harmed if this got out' turns that instinct into a class (F1, F9)

sections.goal: the viewer can explain the difference between public and internal information using a released item and an internal one
concepts: public: approved for release, share freely (F2, F6, F10, F12)
internal: employees only, limited harm, not sent outside without approval (F3, F7, F13)
sections.carrier: two everyday items sorted side by side

sections.goal: the viewer can apply the harm question to the customer list, place it in confidential and use its handling rules: named people who need it, approved protected channels
concepts: confidential: need to know, significant harm (F4, F8)
handling: named recipients, approved channels, protected storage, careful disposal (F14, F15, F16)
sections.carrier: the running customer list classified and its handling shown

sections.goal: the viewer can apply the default rule: when unsure treat it as the higher class and ask the owner; the label travels with the item
concepts: label travels across paper, file and screen (F11)
owner decides; unsure means higher class and ask (F17, F18)
our own policy decides each case (F5)
sections.carrier: one item moving across paper, folder and screen keeping its colour

arc.payoff: back to the Send button: the customer list is confidential, so it goes only if the contractor needs it, by an approved protected channel, and if unsure you ask the list's owner first

practice_ladder.what: press release, meeting notes and the customer list each sorted with the harm question narrated
three items (posted job advert, org chart, payroll file) shown; the viewer sorts them before the answer appears
the viewer decides what to do with the opening email before the narrator says it

recall_moments.prompt_sketch: Sort these three: a posted job advert, the org chart, the payroll file.
recall_moments.tempting_wrong: calling the org chart public because it looks harmless; it is internal unless approved for release (F10)

transfer_tasks: before you attach a file to anything going outside the team, ask who could be harmed if it got out, and check its class

persona.voice: a calm, capable colleague who explains how things work here
persona.delivery_notes: brisk on public and internal, slower on confidential handling, warm on the when-unsure rule

gagne.attention: hook: cursor on Send with a customer list
gagne.recall_prior: bridge from the instinct that some things are sensitive
gagne.present: public, internal, then confidential, in rising harm
gagne.guidance: signature move: item, harm question, then class
gagne.feedback: answer shown with the tempting wrong on the org chart
gagne.assess: payoff: viewer decides the opening email first
gagne.transfer: transfer task: ask the harm question before attaching

merrill.problem_centered: the customer list email is the running problem
merrill.activation: bridge from the existing sense of sensitivity
merrill.demonstration: each class shown on an everyday item before it is named
merrill.application: the three-item sort and the payoff decision
merrill.integration: transfer task and the when-unsure rule

mayer.coherence: only everyday office items; no statistics, laws or tools
mayer.signalling: one colour per class, held throughout; one slowdown on confidential handling
mayer.redundancy: screen shows items, class names and short rules; narration explains
mayer.contiguity: each item's colour changes as its class is spoken
mayer.segmenting: three short sections, one idea each
mayer.pre_training: the harm question is introduced before any class

arcs.relevance: items the viewer handles every week
arcs.satisfaction: the viewer resolves the opening email

flags: No company policy supplied: lesson describes a typical scheme and says our own policy decides each case (F5)
